cards.explanation: The answer is the one who is exiled. The message says, “Weep bitterly for him who is exiled, for he will never return to see his native land.” The dead one is done with the journey, friends. The exiled one has to keep living far from home. I think that's a sad kind of heavy.

The answer is die, and it's a heavy line. The LORD says Shallum, Josiah's son and king of Judah, “…will die in the place to which he was exiled; he will never see this land again.” So the trip out is one way. No return ticket.

The answer is that he makes them serve without pay. The woe falls on the one “…who makes his countrymen serve without pay, and fails to pay their wages…” So the workers swing the hammers and the paycheck never shows up. Not even a late one, friends.

The answer is, “Does it make you a king to excel in cedar?” The man has windows, cedar panels and vermilion paint. The LORD's question is whether any of that is what makes a king. Nice paneling is not the same as being a good king, bakers.

The answer is the poor and needy. The father “…took up the cause of the poor and needy, and so it went well with him.” That's what justice and righteousness looked like for him. He stood up for the people with the least.

The answer is True. After describing the father's care for the poor and needy, the LORD asks, “Is this not what it means to know Me?” So knowing Him is tied to how a person treats people, friends. It's not about how fancy the house is.

The answer is his own dishonest gain. The LORD says, “…your eyes and heart are set on nothing except your own dishonest gain, on shedding innocent blood, on practicing extortion and oppression.” Dishonest gain heads that list. The verse follows it with shedding innocent blood, extortion and oppression.

The answer is False. About Jehoiakim, Josiah's son and king of Judah, the LORD says, “They will not mourn for him…” (Jeremiah 22:18). Cries like “Alas, my master! Alas, his splendor!” are ones they will not make for him. The text goes on to say he will be buried like a donkey, dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 22:19). I think that's a heavy part, friends, so let's take it slowly.

The answer is a donkey. The LORD says, “He will be buried like a donkey, dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem.” It's a heavy picture, and the text doesn't soften it. I think it's meant to show how far from a king's farewell this is.

The answer is that all your lovers have been crushed. The call is to cry out “…for all your lovers have been crushed.” Lebanon, Bashan and Abarim are the places named for the crying out. The text doesn't say who the lovers are, so I'll leave that open, bakers.

The answer is False, and the LORD says it plainly. “This has been your way from youth, that you have not obeyed My voice.” So the refusal goes way back, friends. It's a habit that was built over many years.

The answer is captivity. The LORD says, “The wind will drive away all your shepherds, and your lovers will go into captivity.” The shepherds get driven away and the lovers go into captivity. After that, the text says shame and humiliation follow.

The answer is a woman in labor. The one nestled in the cedars will groan “…when pangs of anguish come upon you, agony like a woman in labor.” It's a comparison for how sharp the pain will be, friends. The text says the groaning is coming.

The answer is False. After swearing, “As surely as I live…” the LORD says that even if Coniah, Jehoiakim's son and king of Judah, were “…a signet ring on My right hand, I would pull you off.” A ring on the right hand sits close, and still He would pull it off. That's a strong word, bakers.

The answer is Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans. The LORD says He will hand Coniah over “…to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and to the Chaldeans.” These are the ones who want to take his life, and he dreads them. They're named plain as day in the verse, friends.

The answer is True. The LORD says He will hurl Coniah and the mother who gave him birth “…into another land, where neither of you were born—and there you both will die.” Mother and son go together, friends. A heavy word, and I think it's one to read slowly.

The answer is a shattered pot. The question asks, “Is this man Coniah a despised and shattered pot, a jar that no one wants?” A broken jar that nobody wants. The very next question asks why he and his descendants are hurled out into a land they do not know.

The answer is as childless. The LORD says, “Enroll this man as childless, a man who will not prosper in his lifetime.” Childless is how the record is to read, friends. The same verse goes on to say that none of his descendants will prosper to sit on the throne of David or to rule again in Judah.

The answer is True. The LORD says, “None of his descendants will prosper to sit on the throne of David or to rule again in Judah.” That's about Coniah's line, bakers. David's throne is named right in the verse.
